content: The 2018 Implementation Guidance titled Protecting, Promoting, and Supporting Breastfeeding in Facilities Providing Maternity and Newborn Services: The Revised Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative was developed collaboratively by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF). This document reflects their joint efforts to improve breastfeeding practices globally, particularly in facilities that provide maternity and newborn care. The guidance emphasizes the critical role of breastfeeding in reducing child mortality, promoting brain development, and protecting against childhood obesity. It also highlights the health benefits for mothers, including reduced risks of breast and ovarian cancers and diabetes. Breastfeeding is presented as a cost-effective intervention that saves lives and reduces healthcare costs. The Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI), launched in 1991, is based on the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding, which were first outlined in a 1989 joint WHO-UNICEF statement. These steps have been implemented in nearly all countries worldwide, with varying degrees of success. However, sustaining the program and achieving universal coverage remain significant challenges. In 2015, WHO and UNICEF initiated a comprehensive review of the BFHI to strengthen its implementation. This process included systematic literature reviews, case studies, interviews, and a global policy survey. The evidence gathered informed the development of updated guidelines and implementation strategies. A BFHI Congress held in 2016 brought together representatives from 130 countries to discuss the future direction of the initiative. The updated guidance includes a revision of the Ten Steps, aligning them with current evidence-based guidelines and global public health policies. The steps are divided into two categories: institutional procedures to ensure consistent and ethical care (critical management procedures) and standards for individual care of mothers and infants (key clinical practices). The guidance also incorporates the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes and emphasizes the importance of ongoing internal monitoring. The document calls for countries to integrate the BFHI into their national healthcare systems to ensure universal implementation of the Ten Steps. It outlines nine key responsibilities for national BFHI programs, including establishing a national coordination body, integrating the Ten Steps into national policies, building the capacity of healthcare professionals, and using external assessments to evaluate adherence. The guidance is intended for policymakers, healthcare facility managers, and professionals involved in maternal and child health programs. It provides practical steps to protect, promote, and support breastfeeding in all facilities, regardless of the country’s economic status or the type of facility (public or private). The ultimate goal is to ensure that all newborns, whether premature or full-term, receive the healthiest start in life through breastfeeding. WHO and UNICEF remain committed to supporting breastfeeding as a vital strategy for improving the survival, nutrition, growth, and development of infants and young children, as well as the health and well-being of mothers. The Ten Steps offer a clear framework for healthcare facilities and workers worldwide to help more mothers breastfeed successfully. Together, these efforts aim to give every newborn the best possible start in life.
